Most Caribbean corals species acquire symbiotic algae during early life from the sediment and water column (Roth 2014). Once acquired, symbionts contribute photosynthetic products to coral cells and can serve as a heterotrophic food source in nutrient-limited conditions (Nitschke et al. 2016; Roth 2014; Wiedenmann et al. 2023). Montipora capi- tata colonies were tagged and mapped at each site, and a range of environmental data including depth, temperature, and sedimentation rate was collected beginning in 2017; full details can be found in (Caruso and Rocha de Souza et al. 2022). nodes.question: What is the mutualistic relationship mentioned in the abstract?
nodes.answer: The mutualistic relationship is between scleractinian corals and dinoflagellate algae from the Family Symbiodiniaceae.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The mutualistic relationship between scleractin- ian corals and dinoflagellate algae (Family Symbiodiniaceae) is critical to the success of corals on tropical reefs yet under - pins their vulnerability to climate change. This symbiosis often deteriorates during marine heatwaves as corals rapidly expel their symbionts, inducing mortality unless symbiosis is restored. While symbiont loss during coral bleaching is well-documented, little is known about symbiont turnover and expulsion under non-bleaching environmental condi- tions. To better understand rates and patterns of symbiont turnover under ambient (non-stressful) conditions, we used a novel methodology to capture and quantify expelled sym- bionts of six Caribbean reef-building coral species. Rep- licate 5-cm2 fragments of Acropora cervicornis, Diploria labyrinthiformis, Montastraea cavernosa, Orbicella faveo- lata, Pseudodiploria clivosa and Siderastrea siderea were incubated in 150 mL of 0.2 m filtered seawater and main- tained at 28 C for 7 h during either day (6:0 h 13:0 h) (110 mol quanta m 2 S 1) or night (18:0 h 1:0 h) con- ditions. Seawater from the incubation chambers was then concentrated and symbionts counted using a hemocytometer.

nodes.question: What factors were found to significantly affect symbiont expulsion rates in corals?
nodes.answer: Symbiont genus, abundance, performance, coral species, and time of day significantly affected symbiont expulsion rates.
nodes.paragraph: Calculated expulsion rates were paired with relative symbi- ont densities in the coral tissue (symbiont/host cell ratios using quantitative PCR) and their photochemical efficiency (Fv/Fm, measured using chlorophyll fluorometry). We found that symbiont expulsion varied significantly by symbiont genus, abundance, performance, coral species, and time of day. Our findings offer insight into coral-Symbiodiniaceae homeostasis, mechanisms of coral-algal symbiosis and dys- biosis, and the potential symbiont availability and spread of symbionts in the environment and have implications for restoration approaches that involve provisioning or seeding corals with algal symbionts. Keywords Coral Symbiosis Symbiodiniaceae Expulsion Caribbean Introduction Coral reefs are integral to ocean health and the welfare of coastal communities globally, supporting a vast array of organisms, connecting tropical and sub-tropical marine ecosystems, protecting coastlines, and fueling fisheries and global tourism industries (Bruckner 2002; Brandl et al. 2019 ; Harborne et al. 2017 ; Needham 2010 ; Pascal et al. 2016). nodes.question: At what temperature were the Symbiodiniaceae cells stored before processing?
nodes.answer: The Symbiodiniaceae cells were stored at 4°C before processing.
nodes.paragraph: The remaining cell pellet was vortexed, removed, and resuspended to a total volume of 1.5 mL using 0.2 m FSW. Lugols solution (10%) was added to preserve the Symbiodiniaceae cells, which were stored at 4 C before being processed on a hemocytometer within two months of collection. Calculating fragment tissue surface area Fragment tissue surface area was calculated in ImageJ (v. 1.51) using photographs collected during sampling. Photographs were uploaded individually to ImageJ and sized so that the entire coral fragment and ruler were visible. The straight segment tool was then utilized to set a scale of a known distance of 1 cm as shown on the ruler in the image (Known Distance = 1, Unit of Length = cm). Once distance was standardized, the polygon selection tool was utilized to trace the circumference of the fragment (massive species) or utilized to trace the diameter and height of the fragment (Acer). The measure tool was then utilized to calculate area for the massive species while the area of the Acer fragments was calculated using the curved surface area of a cylinder (2 rh ) and curved surface area of a cone ( rl ) area calculations to best approximate tissue surface area of the base (cylinder) and tip (cone) of the fragment.

nodes.question: How do corals demonstrate their ability to adapt through symbiont communities?
nodes.answer: Many corals can shift their symbiont communities in favor of Durusdinium after exposure to bleaching, showcasing their ability to acclimatize or adapt through symbiont recombination.
nodes.paragraph: 2020; Hoadley et al. 2019; Silverstein et al. 2017). The rate and magnitude of symbiont mass expulsion depend on the severity of the bleaching stressor, the coral host species and genotype, and the relative abundance and identity of the Symbiodiniaceae it hosts (Cunning and Baker 2013; Silverstein et al. 2017). For instance, corals hosting Durusdinium trenchii are particularly tolerant to bleaching and environmental stress (Chen et al. 2020; Silverstein et al. 2017; van Oppen et al. 2005). Indeed, many corals can shift their symbiont communities in favor of Durusdinium after exposure to bleaching, demonstrating their ability to acclimatize or adapt through symbiont recombination (Baker 2004; Claar et al. 2020). While it is well established that bleaching can drive shifts in symbiont communities, few studies have directly quantified symbiont expulsion as an ongoing regulatory (homeostatic) mechanism of coral-algal symbiosis especially in the absence of heat stress and associated dysbiosis. Previous research has demonstrated that corals routinely expel symbionts into their environment and expulsion rates can vary seasonally and in response to varying temperature and light conditions (Dimond and Carrington 2008; Hoegh-Guldberg et al.
